promptText: As an engineering target, what does 'generalization' mean in the context of intelligent systems?
options: Producing the mathematically correct output for every possible input, without exception
Producing useful outputs for inputs the system has never seen before, without a human writing an explicit rule for each one
Memorizing every training example so it can be recalled exactly at inference time
Reducing the model's parameter count as much as possible while keeping accuracy constant
explanation: A traditional program is a finite, explicit mapping written by a human; an intelligent system must instead produce a reasonable output for inputs outside any table the engineer wrote, which is why the chapter treats generalization as the single most important word in the series.

promptText: What is 'Good Old-Fashioned AI' (GOFAI / Symbolic AI) fundamentally built on?
options: Statistical pattern learning from large amounts of labeled data
Manipulating symbols according to explicit, hand-authored logical rules
Gradient descent optimization of billions of numeric parameters
Predicting the next token in massive, mostly unlabeled text corpora
explanation: Symbolic AI represented knowledge as hand-written facts and rules chained together by an inference engine, which is why it was explainable and auditable but hit the knowledge acquisition bottleneck at scale.

promptText: In the chapter's 'dial-turning' analogy for training, who or what determines how each parameter (dial) is adjusted after an error is measured?
options: A human engineer manually sets each dial based on domain expertise
An automated procedure (backpropagation combined with gradient descent) computes the adjustment directly from the measured error
The dials are adjusted randomly and the best run is kept
The dials are frozen after random initialization and never changed again
explanation: No human decides which dial to turn or by how much — backpropagation and gradient descent compute the adjustment automatically from the loss, which is the mechanical core of what 'learning' means.

promptText: Which of the chapter's three working definitions of intelligence is next-token prediction training most directly built on?
options: Behavioral (Turing) — judged purely by external, human-indistinguishable output
Compression-based — modeling the world well enough to predict what comes next
Agentive — perceiving an environment and taking actions toward goals
Embodied — intelligence requiring a physical body interacting with the world
explanation: The compression-based definition explains why training on 'guess the next word' forces a model to build broad internal representations of how the world works, which is the mechanism underlying pretraining.

promptText: What was the 'knowledge acquisition bottleneck' that limited Symbolic AI and expert systems?
options: A lack of sufficient computing hardware to run rule engines quickly
The need for humans to hand-author and maintain every fact and rule, which doesn't scale to common-sense, real-world domains
Insufficient statistical theory for probability calculations
Too much labeled training data being available for the rules to use
explanation: Every fact and rule had to be manually elicited and entered by a human expert and knowledge engineer, and the number of rules and exceptions needed for real-world coverage grew far faster than authoring throughput could keep up.

promptText: Why does the chapter say a large language model 'is not a function in the mathematical sense you are used to'?
options: Because it internally uses floating-point numbers instead of integers
Because calling it repeatedly with the identical input can produce different, subtly varying outputs
Because it requires specialized hardware (a GPU) to run at all
Because it can only accept text as input, never numbers
explanation: Call reverse('hello') a thousand times and you always get 'olleh'; ask an LLM the same question a thousand times and you can get subtly different answers — this probabilistic behavior is the entire premise the chapter builds on.

promptText: Per the chapter's security discussion, why does prompt injection follow directly and unavoidably from the 'prediction as a proxy for understanding' mechanism?
options: Because models cannot be connected to the internet safely
Because the model has no hard-coded, tamper-proof way to distinguish 'instructions from the developer' from 'text that happens to contain instruction-like phrasing'
Because all models are trained exclusively on public internet text
Because temperature=0 is rarely enforced by API providers
explanation: Unlike a parameterized SQL query, a model has no structural boundary between instructions and data — any untrusted text that reaches it is a potential attack surface, which is the root cause of prompt injection.

promptText: A candidate says: 'The model told me it was very confident in its answer, so I trusted it.' What is the flaw in this reasoning, per the chapter?
options: Confidence-sounding language is generated by the same fluency-driven mechanism as the rest of the output and is not a calibrated signal of accuracy
Models are structurally incapable of ever producing confident-sounding language
Confidence statements are only meaningful for classification tasks, never for open-ended text
The reasoning is actually correct and stated confidence should always be trusted
explanation: Confidence-sounding phrasing is a property of fluent text generation, not a calibrated signal of correctness — models can and do state fabricated facts with high apparent confidence.

promptText: According to the chapter's historical bottleneck table, which older bottleneck does Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) directly re-solve, just relocated to a new era?
options: The compute scarcity bottleneck of the 1970s
The knowledge acquisition bottleneck from Symbolic AI, since LLMs cannot know an organization's private, current data on their own
The feature engineering bottleneck of 1990s statistical ML
The labeled-data bottleneck of purely supervised learning
explanation: The chapter is explicit that nothing was solved for free — the knowledge acquisition bottleneck reappears as the need for RAG, because a model's parametric memory can't cover private or current enterprise facts.

promptText: Why does the chapter argue that 'just keep adding instructions to the prompt' has diminishing and sometimes negative returns, unlike adding a branch to an explicit if/else chain?
options: Because prompts have a hard character limit that can never be exceeded by any provider

Because the model's behavior is not an explicit, inspectable rule chain, so added instructions compete for attention within a finite context window and can interact unpredictably with existing instructions and content
Because every additional instruction causes an automatic syntax error in the prompt
Because model providers charge a separate fee for every instruction added
explanation: Unlike deterministic branching logic, prompt instructions are just more text competing for the model's limited attention, so returns diminish and can even reverse through instruction conflicts or drowned-out signal.

promptText: What does the Chinese Room argument (Searle) illustrate about LLMs, as used in the chapter?
options: That LLMs will inevitably achieve genuine understanding once given enough parameters
That manipulating symbols correctly according to learned statistical rules is not the same as understanding their meaning, which is why hallucination is expected behavior rather than a rare glitch
That processing Chinese text is inherently harder for LLMs than processing English text
That LLMs require a human translator in the loop to process any language
explanation: The argument maps almost literally onto an LLM: fluent, rule-following symbol manipulation with no verified grounding to real-world truth explains why confident, wrong output is the expected behavior of the mechanism, not a bug.

promptText: Why is 'temperature=0' commonly but wrongly assumed to guarantee fully deterministic output from a hosted LLM API?
options: Temperature=0 actually disables API access entirely

Floating-point non-associativity across hardware, provider-side load balancing, and latency optimizations like speculative decoding can still introduce variation even after sampling randomness is removed
Temperature has no relationship to determinism in any system
No provider actually supports setting temperature to zero
explanation: Removing sampling randomness by always picking the top token doesn't remove every other source of variation, which is why teams are surprised when a 'deterministic' temperature=0 pipeline still occasionally varies.

promptText: A VP asks why the team shouldn't just wait for the next model release to fix current reliability problems. Using the chapter's historically-grounded reasoning, what is the strongest counter-argument for investing in evaluation and guardrail infrastructure now?
options: Model releases have effectively stopped happening industry-wide, so waiting is not an option

Every past era (expert systems, statistical ML, deep learning, transformers) still required validation, evaluation, and guardrails suited to its own failure modes — 'wait for the next model' was also the implicit, losing bet during past AI winters
Newer models are always strictly worse than older ones at every task
Evaluation infrastructure becomes worthless the moment a new model version ships, so there is no incentive to build it early
explanation: History shows capability improvements never eliminated the need for engineering discipline around a model, and reliability infrastructure transfers across model upgrades, whereas betting purely on future capability has repeatedly left teams unprepared.

promptText: Combining the compression-based definition of intelligence with the mechanics of gradient-descent training, why is a model's factual accuracy fundamentally decoupled from how fluent or confident it sounds?
options: Because generating fluent text requires strictly more parameters than generating accurate text

Because training minimizes prediction error on plausible next-token continuations, and plausibility is highly correlated with but not identical to truth, so gradient descent applies no direct pressure toward verifying facts
Because confidence is computed by a separate module trained with reinforcement learning in every production model
Because fluency and factual accuracy are measured using the exact same loss function and are therefore mathematically identical
explanation: The training objective only ever rewards statistically plausible continuations; nothing in that objective checks claims against ground truth, so confident and fluent text can be produced regardless of whether it is true.

promptText: Why does the chapter argue that scaling laws favor buying frontier model capability for broad, open-ended tasks, while a small fine-tuned model can still win on a narrow task?
options: Because fine-tuned models are always strictly cheaper to build regardless of task

Because scaling laws describe general pretraining capability, but a model tuned tightly on a narrow data distribution doesn't need to be good at everything — it can match or beat a much larger general model on that narrow slice at a fraction of the latency and cost
Because scaling laws apply only to natural language tasks and never to narrow classification problems
Because frontier models are architecturally incapable of ever being fine-tuned
explanation: Scaling laws reliably favor larger models for raw general capability, but a small model narrowly fine-tuned on your specific distribution avoids paying for breadth it doesn't need, which is the practical crux of the build-vs-buy decision.
